    7. Leaf margin (entire / toothed) AND if toothed (dentate, serrate, etc.)): entire (margins are smooth and continuous, with no visible teeth or serrations)

Locating an individual
It is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Distribution
From Belize to Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is widely distributed in the medium to low elevations of both slopes, in climates ranging from humid to very humid, although it prefers climates with marked seasonality; 0-700-800 m.
Habit
Trees, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown outer bark.
Bark
Outer bark reddish-brown, scaly, inner bark reddish with a pleasant mango scent; white or milky resinous sap.
Leaves
Odd-pinnate leaves, with 7-9 leaflets, elliptical, oblong, or oblong-lanceolate, 5-21 x 4-7.2 cm, apex acuminate to abruptly acuminate, base obtuse to asymmetric, generally glabrous; petiolules without evident pulvini, margin entire; petioles 4-14 cm long.
Flowers
Inflorescences are panicles, 3-15 cm long, axillary. Yellowish or greenish-yellow flowers (unisexual); calyx with 5 lobes, 1-1.5 mm long, cuculiform; petals (tubular corolla), with 5 lobes, 5-5.5 mm long; stamens 10, 1 mm long, filaments inserted at the base of the disc; annular disc with 10 lobes; ovary with 5 lobes, ovoid, with 5 locules; style 1, stigma with 5 lobes.
Fruits
Capsular and drupe-like fruits, 1.5-2.5 x 1.5 x 3 cm, ovoid or more or less turbinate, with 2-5 lobes, dehiscent by 4-5 valves, scarlet red inside, red to black when mature; pyrenes 3-5, 12-13 mm thick, white, the mesocarp (pseudoaril) reddish turning white upon exposure (dehiscence), fleshy, juicy, sweet, and edible.
Diagnosis
Characterized by being a large tree, the bark on mature trees is somewhat scaly, lenticellate, and the inner bark has a very particular and pleasant mango scent. At the vegetative level, it is sometimes confused with the genus Protium, although its leaves lack pulvinated petiolules and the turpentine aroma when crushed. Its fruits are distinctive for their peculiar turbinate shape.
Habitat
In the Forest; it is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Phenology
Flowers observed in June and August; fruits in August and February.

Tree, to 30 m tall and 40 cm dbh (often much shorter along the shore); outer bark hard, closely fissured; inner bark red; younger stems, leaf rachises, and axes of inflorescences densely strigose and puberulent (in Panama) or sparsely strigose, sparsely puberulent, or nearly glabrous (often in South America). Leaves alternate, imparipinnate, mostly 15-30 cm long; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets apparently never dimorphic, usually 5-9 (rarely 3 or 10), usually alternate, ± elliptic, acuminate, obtuse-attenuate at base, 4-21 cm long, 1.5-8 cm wide, usually glabrous or minutely puberulent and/or strigose on midrib on both surfaces, rarely strigose below; midrib sharply raised. Panicles axillary (often appearing terminal), mostly 8-20 cm long; flowers white or greenish-yellow, 4-6-parted, as wide as long, globular in bud, the trichomes (at least on calyx) erect or appressed; calyx saucer-shaped, the lobes acute or blunt; petals valvate, ovate, to ca 2 mm long, glabrous or sparsely appressed-pubescent outside, glabrous inside, the margins papillose-puberulent; staminal tube two-thirds to three-fourths as long as petals, broader than long, glabrous outside and in but sometimes pubescent inside near apex, the lobes narrowly acute; anthers twice as many as petals, very narrowly ovoid, ca 0.5 mm long, alternating with and usually longer than lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, densely appressed-pubescent with white trichomes all over; style usually glabrous. Capsules ellipsoid, 11-18 mm long, orange at maturity, prominently tuberculate, the 3 (4) valves folding back to expose shiny red aril; seeds 1 or 2, smooth, ellipsoid, ca 1 cm long. Abundant as seedlings; common as adults in the forest, especially in the old forest. Flowering is bimodal, but principally from April to June, especially in June; a second but much smaller flowering period may occur from September to November. [unclear reference] The fruits from the first flowering mature mostly during September and October, especially in October; mature fruits from the second flowering have been seen in June.

Locating an individual
Cantarrana, around the station.
Distribution
From Mexico to Brazil. In Costa Rica, widespread in very humid wet forests on both slopes; 0-1,150 m.
Habit
Tree, 10-35 m tall.
Trunk
Cylindrical trunk, with slender, cylindrical, grayish twigs; small stipules attached to the petiole.
Bark
With smooth, grayish bark.
Leaves
Simple, alternate leaves, 2.5-12 x 0.8-5 cm, ovate to oblong, acuminate apex, rounded to cupped base, whitish or grayish on the underside, 5-9 pairs of secondary veins, entire margin; petioles 3-7 mm long.
Flowers
Greenish-yellow flowers, 1.5 mm long, with absent petals and 3-5 stamens. Inflorescences panicles, up to 16 cm long.
Fruits
Fruits drupes, 1.5-1.8 cm long, pear-shaped to ovoid, pink when ripe.
Diagnosis
Distinguished by its clearly bicolored leaves, the underside whitish to grayish and the thin blade with very fine reticulation. Also, by its pear-shaped fruits.
Habitat
Generally observed in forests on rolling terrain.
Phenology
Fruits observed in July.

Dioecious, hemiepiphytic tree, to 10 m tall; trunk to 15 cm dbh; branches spiraled, stiff and spreading, densely rooting at the nodes, the roots often extending back to the host tree and enveloping the host tree for support; stems glabrous with prominent leaf scars; sap pale yellow to bright orange (in time), not copious. Petioles to 2 cm long; blades obovate, rounded at apex (sometimes acute to acuminate on juvenile leaves), acute to obtuse at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-10 cm wide, very thick, dark green and glossy above, dull below, coriaceous; veins indistinct, drying with many fine veins. Panicles stout, bracteated, divaricately branched, terminal; buds depressed-globose; pedicels stout, to 1 cm long; flowers thick, 5-parted, spreading at anthesis, to 4.5 cm diam, white to pink, the lobes often marked with maroon or magenta at base or apex; sepals 2, concave, unequal, persisting in fruit; petals 4-10, broadly oblong, 2-2.5 cm long; androecium of staminate flowers cushion-shaped, ca 1 cm wide and 5 mm high with numerous anthers; pollen white, granular, compressed in round or oval pouches ca 1 mm diam, embedded just beneath the sticky surface of the disk; pistillate flowers similar to staminate but the gynoecium divided into (4)9(15) segments, the petals falling soon after anthesis, the sepals closing. Capsules subglobose, 2.5-3 cm long, dehiscing into 5-9 parts at maturity; valves thick, ± spreading to expose the colorful mass of seeds; seeds numerous, reddish, curved-oblong, ca 5 mm long, embedded in a deeply divided, bright-orange aril. Frequent epiphyte in the forest or on exposed shorelines; epiphytic on rocks or on trees near the edge of the water. Plants are usually supported on tree trunks or large branches but the branches may grow into the top of the canopy. Apparently flowers and fruits sporadically throughout the year. Where plants occur along the shore, the branches usually root at the nodes with the roots hanging in the water. The pollen sacs of the staminate flowers burst under the slightest pressure, and abundant pollen oozes out (sometimes explosively). Several species of small bees, including Trigona spp., have been seen visiting the flowers. The geographical range of Symphonia globulifera extends from Nicaragua to Panama, probably to Colombia. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Colon, San Bias, Veraguas, Herrera, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Code (El Valle) and Panama (Cerro Campana), and from tropical wet forest in Code (La Mesa) and Panama.

Dioecious shrub or tree, to 15 m tall; trunk slender or to 20 cm dbh and deeply invaginated; stems sericeous when very young, glabrate in age, with conspicuous leaf scars. Leaves somewhat clustered at apex of branchlets; stipules caducous, to 1 cm long, sericeous, leaving a conspicuous interpetiolar line of trichomes; petioles 6-14 mm long, sericeous to glabrate; blades ovate-elliptic to obovate-elliptic, abruptly short-acuminate, usually obtuse and ± decurrent onto petiole at base, 7-13(21) cm long, 3.5-8 (12) cm wide, glabrous or with sparse long trichomes on major veins below and tufts of trichomes in axils, the margins ciliate and ± revolute.

Life Form: Tree, Shrub 10. Maquira Aubl. By C.C. Berg. Trees or shrubs, dioecious. Leaves alternate, distichous on lateral branches; blade leathery, margins entire, pinnate-veined; stipules not completely amplexicaul, free. Inflorescences on spurs in the axils of the leaves, unisexual, discoid-capitate, involucrate. Staminate inflorescences often several together, pedunculate; flowers not covered by the inner involucral bracts before anthesis, numerous; perianth 4-parted to 4-divided; stamens 4; pistillode absent. Pistillate inflorescences subsessile; flowers numerous; perianth 4-lobed; ovary adnate to the perianth; stigmas 2, tongue-shaped. Fruit-bearing perianth enlarged, fleshy, orange; fruits adnate to the perianth; seed large, without endosperm, cotyledons thick and equal. 4 spp. Tropical America.

Fruit-bearing perianth enlarged, fleshy, orange; fruits adnate to the perianth; seed large, without endosperm, cotyledons thick and equal. 4 spp. Tropical America.

Life Form: Tree 3. Brosimum Sw., nom. cons. By C.C. Berg. Trees, monoecious or dioecious. Leaves alternate and distichous; blade leathery to chartaceous, entire, pinnate-veined; stipules completely amplexicaul and connate or semi-amplexicaul and free. Inflorescences in the axils of the leaves, bisexual or unisexual, pedunculate; receptacle globose, hemispherical, turbinate or convexly discoid, initially completely covered by peltate bracts. Staminate flowers several to numerous; perianth well developed, vestigial or absent; stamens 1-4; pistillode absent. Pistillate flowers 1-several, embedded in the receptacle; ovary adnate to the perianth; stigmas 2, filiform to vine-like. Fruits forming a drupe along with the enlarged, fleshy, and often colored receptacle. Seed large, without endosperm; cotyledons thick, equal or unequal. Approx. 15 spp. Tropical America.

Life Form: Tree 3. Brosimum Sw., nom. cons. By C.C. Berg. Trees, monoecious or dioecious. Leaves alternate and distichous; blade leathery to chartaceous, entire, pinnate-veined; stipules completely amplexicaul and connate or semi-amplexicaul and free. Inflorescences in the axils of the leaves, bisexual or unisexual, pedunculate; receptacle globose, hemispherical, turbinate or convexly discoid, initially completely covered by peltate bracts. Staminate flowers several to numerous; perianth well developed, vestigial or absent; stamens 1-4; pistillode absent. Pistillate flowers 1-several, embedded in the receptacle; ovary adnate to the perianth; stigmas 2, filiform to vine-like. Fruits forming a drupe along with the enlarged, fleshy, and often colored receptacle. Seed large, without endosperm; cotyledons thick, equal or unequal. Approx. 15 spp. Tropical America.

Tree, 3-8 (15) m tall, 5-35 cm dbh; wood yellow; stems weakly striate, brown or with a thin gray flaky crust, the leaf scars 3-sided, raised. Petioles 5-11 cm long, canaliculate, somewhat swollen at apex; blades ± oblong-elliptic, long-acuminate, obtuse to rounded at base, 10-30 cm long, 5-11 cm wide, glabrous, the midrib raised above. Panicles axillary and terminal, to ca 20 cm long; pedicels to 1.5 cm long; flowers ca 1.2 cm diam, conspicuous and sweetly scented; sepals 3, reflexed at anthesis, caducous; petals 6-12, white, blunt at apex; stamens numerous, unequal, exserted; anthers slightly bifid at apex; style 4-6 mm long; stigma shortly trilobate. Capsules 1-1.5 cm diam, covered with stiff bristles, dehiscing into 3 or 4 parts to expose seed; seed usually solitary, smooth, broadly ovate, ca 7 mm long, flattened on one side, gray-coated, with a shiny, bright red, lateral aril. [Croat 6097, 7753]. Locally abundant along some areas of the shore, especially on the southern side of the island; frequent in the forest. Flowers principally in the rainy season from May to October, rarely as early as April or as late as December. The fruits mature in the early dry season (January to March). Southern Mexico to northern South America. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Chiriqui, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Chiriqui and Panama, and from tropical wet forest in Colon.

Tree, to 30 m tall and 40 cm dbh (often much shorter along the shore); outer bark hard, closely fissured; inner bark red; younger stems, leaf rachises, and axes of inflorescences densely strigose and puberulent (in Panama) or sparsely strigose, sparsely puberulent, or nearly glabrous (often in South America). Leaves alternate, imparipinnate, mostly 15-30 cm long; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs.

Locating an individual
Forest, Tree with plate # 926.
Distribution
From Nicaragua to Colombia and Venezuela. In Costa Rica, widespread in very humid climates of the Caribbean slope and the central part to the southwest of the Pacific slope, 0-750 (-1000) m.
Habit
Tree or shrub, 3-10 m tall.
Leaves
Simple leaves, alternate, 3-17 × 1-6 cm, elliptical, elliptic-oblong or oblanceolate, long acuminate apex, attenuated base, glabrous, margin subentire, crenate or serrate.
Flowers
Yellowish or white-greenish flowers; sepals 4, very small; petals absent; stamens 1. Inflorescences racemose, solitary or 2-3 per axil, 4-14 cm long.
Fruits
Fruit capsule, 3-4 mm long, globose, orange when ripe.
Seeds
Seeds 1 (-3), smooth, with a red to orange aril.
Diagnosis
Characterized by its distichous leaves, with finely serrated margin, relatively thin blade, and fine scalariform tertiary venation. When in bloom, distinguished by its slender and pendulous inflorescence.
Habitat
In the Forest; Central Road (CC).
Phenology
Flowers and fruits observed at the end of August.

Tree, 4.5-35 m, the young twigs minutely adpressed-pubescent to glabrescent. Leaves with the petiole 0.5-1.2 cm; blade 10-30 X 3.5-12 cm, elliptical to oblong-elliptical, acute to obtuse or (rarely) subtruncate at the base, glabrous on the underside, without domatia or (rarely) with countable trichomes in the axils of the main veins, with (4)5-8 secondary veins on each side. Inflorescences [of Nectandra purpurea] 10-17 cm. Flowers with the tepals (1—)1.2—2(—2.4) mm. Fruits 1-1.5 cm, ellipsoidal; cup ca. 0.3 cm. Very wet and pluvial forest, 0-1550 m; Caribbean [vertical] Cords. of Guanacaste, Triarán and Central (E.B. La Selva), San Carlos and Tortuguero Plains, Low Talamanca, both [vertical] Cord. de Talamanca, [Pacific] vertical, S Coastal Range (Fila Cruces). Flowers [of Nectandra purpurea] May-Sept. [in Nicaragua, Bolivia] and [Venezuela], [in the] Guiana [region], [in] Brazil. (Grayum et al. 8898, MO) Nectandra purpurea is recognized by its leaf blades that dry relatively opaque on the adaxial side, with the secondary veins slightly elevated and interconnected, forming a submarginal vein and by its flowers with the tepals densely covered by brown or yellowish trichomes and (usually) with the staminodes conspicuously elevated. The cupules that dry light brown, ± puberulent, are also distinctive.

Guavita cansa-boca, Bribri, Guava, Guava del mono Tree, to 15 m tall; branchlets sparsely strigose when young, glabrate in age, minutely lenticellate, minutely ribbed below petioles (at least when dried). Leaves strigose throughout, especially on axis and midrib of leaflets; petiole and rachis terete to narrowly margined; leaflets in 2 or 3 pairs, lanceolate to elliptic, long-acuminate, acute to rounded at base, the terminal pair 9-18 cm long, 3.5-7.5 cm wide. Spikes axillary, in groups of 1-7; peduncle and rachis strigose; peduncles 2-4 cm long; rachis much shorter, 1-2.5 cm long; bracts subulate, to ± 2 mm long; calyx puberulent, 3-5 mm long, the lobes ± 1 mm long; corolla moderately sericeous, 5-9 mm long, the lobes to 2 mm long; stamens and style to ca 2 cm long. Legumes flat, to 16 cm long and 2 cm wide, minutely puberulent, the margins raised.

Trees or shrubs, dioecious, with white sap; stipules separate and paired (which leave a partial scar on the twig when the stipules fall). Leaves distichous; blade generally serrated, sometimes entire. Inflorescences solitary or paired, spicate or racemose (in Costa Rica), shortly pedunculated. Flowers sessile or pedicellate, the staminate with the perianth 4-parted, the segments imbricate; stamens 4, the filament straight in the bud; pistillate flowers with the perianth tubular, subentire or 4-lobed; ovary free or adnate to the perianth at the base; style 1 with 2 short stigmatic arms. Fruits drupaceous, completely immersed in the growing fleshy perianth. Vegetatively, Sorocea could be confused with Trophis and even with Batocarpus. From the former genus, Trophis, it differs in that Trophis has long and slender stigmas, while Sorocea has short and thick ones; Batocarpus differs by having syncarpous infructescences.

Trees, rarely shrubs; cylindrical trunks, sometimes ribbed or ribbed-interlaced, often with gum, with bark normally scaly and rarely smooth; milky sap, sometimes almost absent in the trunk, rarely yellowish; branching sometimes sympodial (Pouteria); twigs with indumentum of mostly simple trichomes, but sometimes there are Malpighiaceous or dendritic trichomes; stipules normally absent, present in Pouteria (rarely), Ecclinusa, Chromolucuma. Simple leaves, alternate, generally spiral or distichous (Chrysophyllum, Micropholis), secondary venation pinnate or penninerved (Diploon, Micropholis) and tertiary sometimes scalariform (Pradosia, Ecclinusa, Chromolucuma), margin entire; petioles cylindrical thickened towards the base or bottle-shaped, rarely ribbed. Inflorescences are axillary, ramiflorous or cauliflorous, fasciculate, sometimes solitary flowers. Flowers actinomorphic, bisexual or unisexual; sepals in 3 types: 5 unequal, imbricate; 5-12 imbricate; or, 6 in 2 series of 3, valvate; corolla gamopetalous, rotate or tubular, 4-6 (9) lobes; stamens epipetalous 4-6 (12), staminodes sometimes present; gynoecium syncarpous, superior ovary, the locules 1-6 (15); axile placentation, ovules 1 (rarely 2) per locule, simple style. Fruits are berries, rarely drupaceous (Pradosia); seeds 1 to several, the testa hard, smooth, shiny and brown.
The family consists of 53 genera and 1100 species, pantropical; 11 genera and around 408 species in the Neotropics; 10 genera and around 62 species in CR; 3 genera and 12 species in LS. The family is most diverse in lowlands with very humid climates, mainly below 1000 m.
It is recognized by its tree habit, with simple, alternate leaves, without stipules (very rarely present in CR), leaves clustered towards the apex of the twigs, cylindrical petioles thickened towards the base and the presence of milky sap. Venation patterns are of great taxonomic importance, so a careful analysis of them provides much utility in identification, especially the tertiary venation often reticulate at various levels or scalariform. The small flowers show a very homogeneous appearance and are always axillary, generally in fascicles. The seeds are very distinctive for their shape, hardness, luster, and annular scar, the latter variable in shape among genera. The vegetative characteristics mentioned earlier could confuse this family, especially with those that have milky sap, with families such as Olacaceae, Apocynaceae (with alternate leaves), etc.; the inner bark and sap with an almond scent also help to recognize Sapotaceae.
Several species produce edible fruits of economic importance, such as sapote (Pouteria zapota), medlar or sapodilla (Manilkara chicle, M. sapota), caimito (Chrysophyllum cainito), etc. The latex of Manilkara zapota was the primary resource for chewing gum. It is well known that the wood of several species is preferred for its hardness and durability.

Trees, rarely shrubs; cylindrical trunks, sometimes ribbed or ribbed-interlaced, often with gum, with bark normally scaly and rarely smooth; milky sap, sometimes almost absent in the trunk, rarely yellowish; branching sometimes sympodial (Pouteria); twigs with indumentum of mostly simple trichomes, but sometimes there are Malpighiaceous or dendritic trichomes; stipules normally absent, present in Pouteria (rarely), Ecclinusa, Chromolucuma. Simple leaves, alternate, generally spiral or distichous (Chrysophyllum, Micropholis), secondary venation pinnate or penninerved (Diploon, Micropholis) and tertiary sometimes scalariform (Pradosia, Ecclinusa, Chromolucuma), margin entire; petioles cylindrical thickened towards the base or bottle-shaped, rarely ribbed. Inflorescences are axillary, ramiflorous or cauliflorous, fasciculate, sometimes solitary flowers. Flowers actinomorphic, bisexual or unisexual; sepals in 3 types: 5 unequal, imbricate; 5-12 imbricate; or, 6 in 2 series of 3, valvate; corolla gamopetalous, rotate or tubular, 4-6 (9) lobes; stamens epipetalous 4-6 (12), staminodes sometimes present; gynoecium syncarpous, superior ovary, the locules 1-6 (15); axile placentation, ovules 1 (rarely 2) per locule, simple style. Fruits are berries, rarely drupaceous (Pradosia); seeds 1 to several, the testa hard, smooth, shiny and brown.
The family consists of 53 genera and 1100 species, pantropical; 11 genera and around 408 species in the Neotropics; 10 genera and around 62 species in CR; 3 genera and 12 species in LS. The family is most diverse in lowlands with very humid climates, mainly below 1000 m.
It is recognized by its tree habit, with simple, alternate leaves, without stipules (very rarely present in CR), leaves clustered towards the apex of the twigs, cylindrical petioles thickened towards the base and the presence of milky sap. Venation patterns are of great taxonomic importance, so a careful analysis of them provides much utility in identification, especially the tertiary venation often reticulate at various levels or scalariform. The small flowers show a very homogeneous appearance and are always axillary, generally in fascicles. The seeds are very distinctive for their shape, hardness, luster, and annular scar, the latter variable in shape among genera. The vegetative characteristics mentioned earlier could confuse this family, especially with those that have milky sap, with families such as Olacaceae, Apocynaceae (with alternate leaves), etc.; the inner bark and sap with an almond scent also help to recognize Sapotaceae.
Several species produce edible fruits of economic importance, such as sapote (Pouteria zapota), medlar or sapodilla (Manilkara chicle, M. sapota), caimito (Chrysophyllum cainito), etc. The latex of Manilkara zapota was the primary resource for chewing gum. It is well known that the wood of several species is preferred for its hardness and durability.

Shrub or tree, 1-10(-18) m, the twigs brown; stipules deciduous (but sometimes present with submature leaves). Leaves opposite or with a cuspidate apex, often puberulent and (often) entire or serrated (with the glands of the teeth). Petiole 0.2-0.4 cm, lamina 3.5-11 cm, also hirsute on the midrib on the underside. Flowers with the pedicel articulated at the base; sepals 1/4-1/3 the length of the petals, acute to rounded at the apex, indistinctly 1-3-nerved; petals whitish to pale yellow or orange, 3.5-4.2 mm, glabrous or glabrate; stamens with the connective scale extended laterally and apically (< the total length of the anther), subentire; style 1.252 mm. Fruits 1.5-1.9 cm, slightly velvety; seeds 4-8 mm, glabrous. Wet and very wet forest, 0-600+ m; Caribbean slope and near the Continental Divide, Cordilleras of Guanacaste and Talamanca, Plains of Los Guatusos, Tortuguero, and Santa Clara, Lower Talamanca, Pacific slope North Cordillera of Talamanca (Cerro Nara), South Nicoya Peninsula, Parque Nacional Carara, Puriscal region (Parque Nacional La Cangreja), vicinity of Palmar Norte, Gulf Dulce region, Burica Peninsula. Fl. Jan., Mar.—May, Jul., Nov. Southeastern Honduras—Panama. The fruits with the pedicel articulated at the base and glabrous seeds easily distinguish Rinorea squamata from its congeners in Costa Rica with opposite leaves. Due to its densely puberulent leaf blades and (often) also hirsute on the midrib on the underside, Rinorea squamata is somewhat similar to Rinorea sylvatica, but vegetatively very different due to its smaller stipules and blades with the glands of the acicular teeth (versus broadly conical).
